classification_signals: The abstract states: 'this paper reviews the previous research about high-rise buildings' open spaces in the area of brain science and cognitive neuroscience.' (p.3)

Section 1.2 'Research methodology' explicitly states: 'Instead of focusing on functional attributes, this paper reviews the previous research about high-rise buildings' open spaces in the area of brain science and cognitive neuroscience. By analyzing the previous research about brain imaging analysis with fMRI, the research (1) summarizes the aesthetic attributes... (2) analyzes human's preferences... (3) concludes the research findings of the previous study...' (p.3)
The paper synthesizes findings from numerous cited studies and presents them in tables (e.g., Table 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) rather than presenting new empirical data from its own experiments.
The conclusion (IV.5) summarizes findings derived from 'interdisciplinary theoretical knowledge' and 'survey and analysis of the literature on brain response' (p.9).
title: Designing Open Spaces in High-rise Buildings: A Study Based on Neuroesthetics

limitations: The paper does not explicitly state limitations for its own review methodology or scope. It synthesizes findings from other studies, so its limitations would implicitly be those of the reviewed literature.
minimum_safe_summary: This systematic review investigates human preferences for aesthetic attributes in high-rise building open spaces from a neuroesthetics perspective. It synthesizes findings from previous brain science and cognitive neuroscience research, particularly fMRI studies, to identify design considerations. Key findings indicate that natural landscapes, especially mountain and water scenery, significantly improve perceived restoration and attention restoration compared to urban or forest landscapes. Openness, achieved through large windows, wide platforms, and high ceilings (optimally 3.04m), enhances aesthetic pleasure and facilitates spatial exploration by activating specific brain regions. The review also highlights the positive impact of implicit natural elements, such as curved lines and fractal patterns, on preference and neural processing efficiency. The paper proposes direct and fractal methods for integrating natural landscapes into high-rise open space design. No explicit limitations for the review itself were stated, but it relies on the scope and quality of the synthesized literature.
